title: Knowledge Check 2: Lessons 9-16
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 9-16 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Why must an integration make its create operations idempotent before it retries them?
options: It confirms that the downstream service is currently online and healthy
It makes a replayed operation produce the same result every time
It removes the need to log failures for any later review
It turns a transient error into a permanent failure
questions.explanation: Idempotency means an operation yields the same result whether it runs once or many times, so a retry cannot create a duplicate record.

questions.question: A message keeps failing and finally exhausts its retry budget. What should happen to it?
options: Retry the message indefinitely until the service recovers
Drop the message so the queue does not stay blocked
Route the message to a dead-letter channel with an owner
Lower its priority and leave it waiting in the queue
questions.explanation: Once a message exhausts its retry budget without succeeding, it is treated as poisoned and moved to a dead-letter channel where it has a record and an owner.

questions.question: A composite call returns HTTP 200 even though a subrequest failed and rolled back. What does a correct handler do?
options: Treat the 200 status as proof the whole call succeeded
Retry the entire call with exponential backoff
Route the call straight to the dead-letter channel
Inspect the response body for failed subrequests
questions.explanation: A composite request can return HTTP 200 while individual subrequests fail and roll back, so correctness depends on reading the response body, not only the status code.

questions.question: When is a synchronous call the right choice for a step in a pipeline?
options: When the caller needs the result before it can continue
When the caller wants to keep working while the work runs
When the downstream system is slow or frequently down
When the work is high volume and low priority
questions.explanation: A synchronous call blocks the caller for the full round trip, which is the right trade when the caller cannot proceed without the result.

questions.question: What does placing a message queue between a producer and a consumer provide?
options: It guarantees every message is delivered exactly once
It makes the producer wait for each consumer response
It buffers bursts so each side can run at its own pace
It removes the need for any consumer-side error handling
questions.explanation: A queue decouples producer and consumer by buffering bursts, so a slow or busy consumer does not force the producer to wait or flood it.

questions.question: A consumer reads a status immediately after an update and briefly sees an older value. What does this illustrate?
options: A poisoned message that must be retried with exponential backoff
A dead-letter channel holding the update for review
A failed idempotency check performed on the read
An inconsistency window in an eventually consistent system
questions.explanation: When work flows through queues and replicas, a read can briefly lag the latest write, which is the inconsistency window that eventual consistency accepts.

questions.question: How should org-wide defaults be set for an object?
options: To the widest access any user might eventually need across the org
To the most restricted level the most limited user should see
To mirror the role hierarchy exactly, branch for branch
To Public Read Write so sharing rules can restrict later
questions.explanation: Org-wide defaults should express what the most restricted user should see; the other sharing tools can only open access from that floor.

questions.question: Two users sit at the same level of the role hierarchy. Does one automatically see the other's records?
options: Yes, because peers in a role always share each other's records
Yes, if they both report to the same manager
No, access flows up the hierarchy but not between peers
No, unless the object is set to Public Read Write
questions.explanation: The role hierarchy grants a manager the access of the people below, but peers in the same role do not inherit each other's records.

questions.question: A single record was shared manually with an auditor, and then the record's owner is transferred. What happens to that share?
options: The share persists because it names the auditor
The share is upgraded to a sharing rule
The share is preserved for the new owner
The share is dropped when the owner changes
questions.explanation: A manual share is tied to the owner's context, so changing the record's owner removes the share.

questions.question: What is the recommended way to grant the access differences among users?
options: Clone a separate profile for every user and job title
Put every needed permission directly into each user's own profile
Layer task-scoped permission sets over a shared baseline profile
Give each team its own complete copy of the standard profile
questions.explanation: Profiles hold the one-per-user baseline, and task-focused permission sets carry the differences so you avoid profile explosion and reuse grants across users.

questions.question: A permission is disabled in a user's profile but enabled in one of their permission sets. What access does the user have?
options: They have it, because permissions from a set stack
They lose it because the profile is authoritative
They get it only once the profile is edited
They get nothing until a permission set group is added
questions.explanation: Permissions from profiles and permission sets combine, so a grant enabled in a set is effective even when the profile leaves it disabled.

questions.question: Which users are required to use phishing-resistant MFA rather than standard MFA?
options: Every user who signs in through single sign-on from anywhere
Only external community users who log in
Only users who log in from outside the office network
Users holding privileged permissions such as Modify All Data
questions.explanation: Users who hold privileged permissions such as Modify All Data or the System Administrator profile must use phishing-resistant MFA.

questions.question: Which OAuth flow fits a server-to-server integration that has no interactive user?
options: The username-password flow, because it is the simplest to set up
The web server flow, because it returns an authorization code
A server-to-server flow such as JWT bearer or client credentials
The user-agent flow, because it needs no backend service
questions.explanation: Server-to-server flows such as JWT bearer and client credentials need no interactive login, so they fit a machine caller and are not subject to interactive MFA.

questions.question: Why is the username-password OAuth flow discouraged?
options: It requires a browser login that the client cannot perform
It passes user credentials back and forth on each call
It cannot issue access tokens at all
It is limited to a single concurrent user at a time
questions.explanation: The username-password flow sends a user's credentials to the token endpoint on each call, which is why it is discouraged and should be blocked on apps.

questions.question: A company wants customers and partners to log into a portal. Which approach fits, and which one is the anti-pattern?
options: A community with internal Salesforce licenses, to save cost
A connected app with the username-password flow
A single sign-on setting that points partners at employee roles
A community with external licenses, never internal ones
questions.explanation: External customers and partners belong on Experience Cloud sites with external licenses; using internal licenses for outside users is explicitly discouraged.

questions.question: How do you model a many-to-many relationship between two objects?
options: A single lookup field on each of the two related objects
A formula field that summarizes the parent object
A junction object with two master-detail relationships
A record type defined on each of the two objects
questions.explanation: Salesforce grants no direct many-to-many field, so you model it with a junction object that holds two master-detail relationships, one to each side.

questions.question: Which situation best describes data skew?
options: Too many records concentrated on one parent or owner
Records duplicated across Salesforce and an external system
Fields populated with inconsistent formatting
Reports that exceed their row limits
questions.explanation: Data skew is the concentration of records on a single parent, owner, or lookup target, which turns brief locks into contention and failed saves at volume.

questions.question: A bulk integration writes to a lookup target that hundreds of thousands of records already point at, and saves start throwing lock exceptions. What is the fix?
options: Add many more child records to spread the lock out more widely
Distribute the values across more targets or use a picklist
Remove the owner from the record so it stops locking
Increase the lookup field length to reduce contention
questions.explanation: Lookup skew is eased by reducing lock frequency and duration, such as spreading the associated records across more values or replacing the object with a picklist.

questions.question: What does an embedding capture about a piece of content?
options: The exact wording of a document, character for character
The semantic meaning of content as a list of numbers
The access permissions attached to a source document
The version history of a source document
questions.explanation: An embedding represents meaning as a vector of numbers, so similarity can be compared mathematically rather than by matching exact words.

questions.question: In a retrieval-augmented knowledge base, which component is the source of truth?
options: The embedding vector most recently generated for the chunk
The metadata attached to each chunk in the store
The vector database's similarity scores at query time
The original source documents the index was built from
questions.explanation: The vector store is a derived artifact; the original documents remain the system of record and the index must be refreshed when they change.

questions.question: Why does changing the embedding model count as a migration rather than a simple toggle?
options: Stored vectors stop matching, so they need re-embedding
The database license must be renewed for the newer model
The metadata field names change automatically
The similarity metric is disabled during the change
questions.explanation: Changing the embedding model moves the semantic space, so every stored vector must be re-embedded and cut over like a schema change.

questions.question: What is the key difference between ETL and ELT?
options: ETL uses external IDs and ELT does not use them
ETL loads raw data and ELT cleans it before loading
ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw then transforms
ETL is only for Salesforce and ELT only for cloud data lakes
questions.explanation: ETL performs transformation on a separate step before loading, while ELT loads raw data into the target first and transforms it there; the difference is where the middle step runs.

questions.question: In what order should dependent objects be loaded during a migration?
options: Parents before children, so required lookups resolve
Children before parents, to load the highest volume first
Alphabetically by object name
In whatever order the export files were generated
questions.explanation: Objects with mandatory relationships must load parents before children, or a child's relationship field has nothing to point at.

questions.question: How do external ID fields help preserve data integrity during a migration?
options: They increase the per-import record limit for every single object load
They encrypt the source data during the load process
They replace the need for a backup before loading
They preserve relationships and enable upsert without duplicates
questions.explanation: External ID fields carry the source system's key, so the loader can resolve relationships across separate files and upsert without creating duplicates.
